records.title: Show HN: It's now easy to install Linux on an Android Phone – Android2linux
records.author: brazukadev
records.storyText:
Hey HN!

One of my biggest dreams (really) was to have a Linux phone. I tried to install on some phones in the past, even the ones that would be marked as compatible and it was always so difficult that I couldn't really do it. Yesterday I decided to try again, this time using Claude to do most of the work. A couple hours later it runs postmarketOS as my second phone: 4G, SMS, a terminal, SSH.

It took two fixes. U-Boot didn't recognise my phone model, so I patched 14 bytes of its device-tree match strings. Then the modem wasn't working, because the packaged TFTP server that lends the modem a folder mishandled its file-size queries but an upstream build fixed it.

The repo is what came out of it: guides for any phone (but specific just for my xiaomi), an agent skill that follows the same method and safety rules, notes per phone, and web apps reworked for a phone screen (WhatsApp Web for desktop with a one-pane layout).

What doesn't work (in this phone of mine): no charger driver yet (slow charging), no cameras, and no banking apps, so I keep an Android at home for those. Whether this works for you depends on your phone having a port. reports through the issue forms help, especially for phones that don't work yet.

I think that finally succeeding at having a Linux phone is worth creating a post on HN. I was thinking about a Tell HN but decided to convert the knowledge into a repo so more people can share, discuss, add their phones, new apps, etc. Hope it helps!

Hey HN,

I've been working on rmux, an open source terminal workspace built in Rust using GPUI and Ghostty's terminal engine.

The main focus has been performance. I wanted something that could handle multiple projects, shells and coding agents without becoming a resource hog or feeling sluggish as more panes are opened, which has been a frustration I've had with some other terminals.

records.author: yelarys
records.storyText:
A 211M-param transformer acts as a game engine. It draws every next frame from the last 2.4 seconds and my inputs.

Built a simulator of 18 Backrooms levels in PyTorch to generate the data.

Recorded 440 hours of scripted play in it.

Trained the model from scratch on that, using flow matching in a pretrained autoencoder's latent space.

The model was trained on its own imperfect frames as context so it doesn't drift right away. It recalls a few older frames by position, so a quick look back usually works.

Inspired by Oasis Minecraft.

To try it you need an NVIDIA GPU with ~4 GB.

records.title: Show HN: Ripcloc – cloc every edit your agent makes
records.author: kevsten
records.storyText:
Hey HN.

ripcloc exists because I ask agents to consider line cost in feedback early and often when they're doing work to help constrain unnecessary complexity and to trigger discussions about code smells that lead to bad architecture.

It is fast enough that you can add it to a git commit hook. It is fast enough that your agent harness can run it after every tool call.

The other reason it exists is to help _count your tests_.

Ripcloc attributes each line as either a source line, a test line or a comment/doc line, so that you can have a better idea quickly how much your codebase is _implementation_ vs _tests_.

It does this even for inline tests like `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { ... }` in Rust (and is still faster than its predecessors!).

records.title: Show HN: Craoli – find jobs without bias and manipulation from the platforms
records.author: thanouil1411
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I have build a tool after my own job searching. You describe the job you want in a sentence, like "backend roles in Zurich, Python, no banks", and it searches the web and companies' own career pages for it. There is no bias, no curated lists, no promotion; only a pure and powerful search. I wanted to get the real postings. The same jobs can show up to many boards and recruiter sites, often after it's closed. Don't you want to know this? Craoli tries to find the employer's own postings, shows one card for all the copies that exist out there, and keeps checking whether the job is still open.

Another issue I had was that one company while I submitted my job application, changed the job description, by adding one more requirement that was not there when I have applied!! Good luck proving that. Of course the recruiter brought this point for my rejection, that I was sure that it was not there when I applied. 7+ years of pre-sales is hard to miss on a job description when read.

There are some limits for now; career pages are read directly only for the common hiring systems; a custom site is only found through web search. And every search costs me real money, so you need an account, and free has 2 searches a month using a cheaper LLM model; the search costs the same. Additional classical features are there for you to discover, like tailored CVs and cover letters.

What I would like to know: the last time you looked for a job, what made you stop trusting a listing?

records.title: Show HN: Hubbub – Read big HN threads by topic
records.author: roansh
records.storyText:
Hi everyone!

Thank you all for the discussions here. They're the reason I visit and read HN every day.

Big threads are hard to follow. I wanted to see what people are actually talking about before diving in, so I had Opus 5.5 build me a Chrome extension.

On a thread page, Hubbub groups the top-level comments into a handful of topics, with a bar showing how much of the discussion each one takes up. Open a topic and you read the real comments btw, no AI summary. Haiku only groups comments, generates labels, and describes a topic in a sentence or two.

There's a live demo on the landing page: https://hubbub.page

How it works: a small server makes trees ahead of time for front-page threads with 30+ comments, and refreshes them as the threads grow. Every user downloads the same file, so the server can't tell which threads you read. There's no account and no analytics, and your read history stays in your browser.

Do give it a try, let me know if you spot any bugs, or have any feature requests :)

records.title: Show HN: Quadrivia – Trivia for the Intellectually Curious
records.author: jchaykow
records.storyText:
I made Quadrivia, a trivia game covering science, math, logic, nature, geography, and philosophy.

I had the idea about ten years ago. I like trivia, but I don't know much about pop culture, so I wanted a game built for subjects I enjoy. I started writing down questions in my phone's Notes app and reading them to my friends. That eventually became this app.

I put a ton of care into the question creation. The questions are the game. Some reward knowing something interesting, whilst others give you a foothold to reason toward the answer. Building that balance is the hardest part, but when you see the a-ha moment on players faces you begin to understand why the question design is so important.

The game can be played solo but is meant to be played with friends around a table or over FaceTime. You earn "citations" across fields of knowledge and the first to an h-index of 4 wins the game.

The app is free to download with a started question set that supports complete games.

If you're interested in the name: Trivia comes from "Trivium" which in Medieval education were the three foundational subjects (Grammar, Logic, and Rhetoric). Similarly, Quadrivia comes from "Quadrivium" which in Roman times referred to the four mathematical disciplines (Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, and Astronomy).

records.title: Show HN: RayClay – an open source C app framework for desktop, mobile, and web
records.author: impizulu
records.storyText:
RayClay aims to be the most developer-friendly framework for creating native desktop and mobile applications. It handles all the DIY aspects of C for you while retaining all the performance benefits of using a low-level programming language.

MY MOTIVATION

At the start of the year I decided I wanted to develop my own app with the goal of releasing it on mobile, desktop, and web.

Probably like most developers, I wanted to build a closed-source app and distribute it to whomever I wanted. And I didn't want to have to pay any sort of fee or owe any conditions to the development tools I used. It turns out, this set of criteria really limited what framework I could choose.

Distributing it to whomever I wanted meant that the app had to be properly cross-platform. This cut out options like React Native (no official Linux) and Electron (no iOS or Android). And, while Tauri has yeses for all platforms, I decided that its dependence on platform-native webviews would probably mean excessive ongoing maintenance which I would prefer not to have to deal with. These frameworks were all very bloated anyways so it didn't feel like a big loss tbh.

So I was left with choosing between Qt and Flutter, but Qt has this finicky dual licensing model and Flutter still felt a bit too bloated.

Ultimately, I realised that I was looking for a framework that didn't exist: lightweight like Qt but also convenient and fully open-source like Flutter. I wanted the performance of a lower-level framework with the convenience of less-performant frameworks. Is that really so much to ask for :/

This led me to develop RayClay. It's already 6 months old but now I feel it is really ready for the world to check it out since I've released v1.0 (which I deliberately held back releasing until I though it was ready).

This description is adapted from my blog post here https://www.impizulu.com/blog/why-i-built-rayclay where I give a little more detail.

records.title: Show HN: Cordium – FOSS sandbox platform on Kubernetes to eliminate credentials
records.author: geoctl
records.storyText:
Hello HN. Cordium is a FOSS, self-hosted, identity-based, general-purpose sandbox platform built on Kubernetes. The main differentiator here is that Cordium automatically assigns an identity to each sandbox to provide "secretless" secure remote/zero-trust access to resources/infrastructure (e.g. APIs, SSH, databases, k8s, etc.) without having to hold credentials and secrets (e.g. API keys and access tokens, SSH private keys/passwords, database passwords, mTLS private keys, etc.) inside the sandbox.

The way it works is that every Cordium sandbox includes an Octelium ZTNA client (see https://github.com/octelium/octelium) which routes requests from the sandbox to the upstream resources through the Octelium Cluster running on the same underlying Kubernetes cluster over WireGuard tunnels. In the Octelium Cluster, each upstream resource is protected by a corresponding identity-aware proxy that actually holds the upstream credential that injects the credential on-the-fly to the upstream if the downstream (i.e. the Cordium sandbox) is authorized by an Octelium policy.

In short, Cordium is basically a sandbox platform with a dual nature: it doesn't just provide isolated execution runtimes but it also provides and identity and access infrastructure to provide secure secretless remote access, identity management, L7-aware access control and visibility for every request originating from within the sandbox. You can use it for various use cases from a personal self-hosted GitHub Codespaces alternative for remote development as well as a scalable sandbox platform for AI agents to access infrastructure without handling them your credentials at scale. You can also use it as an infrastructure layer to build more complex applications such as agent meshes.

The main features include declarative management, Templates and prebuilds, persistent, ephemeral and forkable storage via Kubernetes volume snapshots, lifecycle tasks, controls such as linux caps, read-only filesystem and egress control, access and management over web portal/SSH/CLI as well as SDKs in Go/Rust/Python/Typescript. You can learn more about Cordium, its features in detail and how it works, please visit the docs at https://octelium.com/docs/cordium/latest/overview/intro

You can also try a live demo for the Cordium web portal at https://demo.octelium.com/cordium and a CLI playground at https://demo.octelium.com/cli

records.title: Show HN: A free website check that starts from what your buyers search
records.author: 4ugusta
records.storyText:
I made Admiral. It is a tool to check that Google and Meta ads are working properly. This is its free website check: you don't need an account and no changes will happen on your site. It will ask for a website URL and it will tell you 6 things about it. Each of the 6 is one sentence. If it is "Good" then no change is needed. If it is "Worth fixing" then it says what is wrong.

1. Where you are in search. Admiral will read your pages and tell you, for the searches someone might type in Google to find you, whether you are in the first page on Google. If Admiral cannot work out which words someone might type, it will say that instead of guessing.

2. Whether AI assistants can read your home page. All websites can write a "robots.txt" file that controls what automated search engines and AI assistants are allowed to read. Admiral will read your file to show you which AI assistants are not allowed to read your home page. It cannot ask them any questions so it does not know what they will say about you.

3. Whether your home page will say what your business is. A website can have a hidden message, called "structured data", that tells a web search engine "This page is about a dental clinic in Leeds". Admiral will check whether your home page has this hidden tag for what kind of business you are and what the location is.

4. How fast is your home page on a phone? Google publishes how long each web page took to show during a real visit on Chrome, for websites with enough visitors (the Chrome UX Report). If your site is in there Admiral will use these numbers, if it isn't then it will time its own visit. Also checks if the phone number can be tapped to call.

5. On the main page (homepage), where is the main button? Is the "book now" or "buy" button on the first screen (a screenshot of the homepage)?

6. Is anything checking how much you earn from the advert? It searches for a Google tag or a Meta pixel (these are small pieces of code that ad platforms use to know whether a visit to your website was an enquiry or a sale)

Things you should know about this:

Uses a Google search in your home country. If it's in the US, India, UK, Canada, Australia, Singapore or the UAE that's fine. If it's in any other country, or where this is not possible, a different search engine will be used and it will let you know that this is what another country may see. Only reads your homepage and up to 7 other pages (links off your homepage) and not the whole website. Only reports with sentences instead of a score out of 100. Admiral is paid software, this is free and Admiral is not required. Very interested to hear about the first "what a customer would type" search that gets it wrong on your site.

Hey HN,

I originally made this game as a bit of fun between some friends and family. Turned out they quite enjoyed it and encouraged me to share it around a bit.

Everyone in your group is given the same 15 letters, you're given five minutes to find the best words you can with the letters provided, scrabble style scoring. One of the letters is a 2x tile, that will double your points for that word.

Longer words get additional bonuses, as well as additional bonuses in the group for longest word and most words.

There's also a daily "global dawdle" where you can see what the best score you can get is for the day, compared vs everyone else in the world who plays that day. This is good if you don't have a group to play with yet.

No accounts needed, free to play. Love to hear what you think!

records.title: Show HN: Coma – Bilingual ES/EN language with LLVM back end and C runtime
records.author: Agmine
records.storyText:
Hey there...! Awkward silence

Okay, I’m not famous yet... Umm... Well. How are you guys doing? Did you eat your lentils? I didn’t, I think they’re gross.

Anyway, today I’m writing this unprofessional, attitude-filled abomination of a post to talk about .Coma, the bilingual ES/EN programming language that goes from Nim to LLVM (native binary) and is capable of competing against C (a knife fight to the death xd). And yes, I’m only 14 years old—so I’m definitely going to flex that and I don’t care what anyone says :).

Alright, enough jokes.

Why did I create .Coma? I created .Coma because I felt decent programming languages are unnecessarily complicated—why not translate a script simpler than a Python script down to low level? Without the famous Garbage Collector, simple, human, and readable.

Why is it called .Coma? I chose the name .Coma because on day one it sounded so bad I wanted it, and then I found tons of meanings—initially it was just Coma, and I added that `.` because it’s like C++ or C#, a joke about the C family’s need to tack a weird symbol onto the end, except instead of at the end it’s at the start. Plus, "Coma" in Spanish is literally "," which with the `.` sounds like `;`, which is the exact thing that doesn’t exist in this language, along with other weird symbols.

My motivations? I want to build something bigger in the future, make systems so good—first to show off :), second, to create a wide range of compatibility and a friendly network for everyone; I want to do this because I like it and I want to change the world, that’s my motivation.

What's my goal here? I want you to clone this GitHub repo, tear it apart, and humble my ego until I can't even get out of bed. Why? So I can fix it. I want you to criticize everything and break all my code—just send it my way, and I'll fix it.

Anyway, here are the links: - GitHub: https://github.com/Agm1ne/.Coma - Product Hunt: https://www.producthunt.com/products/coma-2?launch=coma-2

And with that I’m signing off. Bye-bye!

records.title: Show HN: Tartelette – an RP2040 emulator and breakout simulator
records.author: _pferreir_
records.storyText:
This is something I made (with LLM help) in order to easily develop and test firmware for Eurorack modules.

The RP2040 is the MCU in the famous Raspberry Pi Pico (and Pico W) boards, as well as many other variants and clones. It is a staple of the maker, retro and synth scenes and, while there are already a couple of emulators out there for it, I couldn't find any which allowed me to test my firmware with (simualted) electronics attached. Tartelette lets you connect LEDs, screens, DACs and a growing list of other peripherals to your MCU, and has also limited support for the WiFi/BLE chip in the Pico W. It can run the MicroPython examples as well as a whole lot of other firmware.

It also compiles to WASM and runs on the browser (although some functions such as bridging to the internet won't work).

records.title: Show HN: MemFiddle
records.author: memalign
records.storyText:
Inspired by JSFiddle, I wondered if it'd be possible to make a mobile-optimized experience where I can paste in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript (generated by my favorite LLM) and run that mini web app with ease.

It is possible! Introducing MemFiddle, a way to preview and test simple web apps right in your web browser. You can also add MemFiddle to your home screen as a PWA.

To get started, prompt your favorite LLM (such as ChatGPT) to give you 'HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript with no dependencies' and then paste the resulting file content into MemFiddle.

I created MemFiddle after I convinced my 4-year-old to poop in an unfamiliar place by making a “poop app” together (one-shotting it with ChatGPT on my phone while under duress). I included Poop App as one of the examples in MemFiddle. Full story: https://memalign.github.io/p/poop-app.html

records.title: Show HN: Custom SQLites for agents (a remote MCP)
records.author: tukkajukka
records.storyText:
What if your agents could create (almost) any SQLite database they need?

I built databasedmcp to let Claude (or any other agent) create databases for my sessions, in both Claude and Claude Code.

With the MCP, agents can create multiple databases with basically any schema.

Docs and tool descriptions: https://databasedmcp.com/docs

Some use cases that I've discovered:

* Share data between agents

Let agents store their status, what they're working on, etc. This is essentially about passing data between coding agents.

E.g. set up a worker agent that picks up work items that other agents add to the database. This kind of enables autonomous work discovery.

* Build custom apps

I've built many ad-hoc apps just by describing the idea to Claude. Ask it to create the UI as an artifact and to use databasedmcp as the backend.

Artifacts can call MCP tools however they want. You use the chat to modify the app, and use the app itself in the artifact UI.

Pretty easy to build small apps such as a shopping list, an expense tracker, etc. Then use Claude to extract data from documents, and store the data with databasedmcp in a structured manner.

Any comments are appreciated, thanks!

records.title: Show HN: Jam – A music making game where you play gigs to earn studio gear
records.author: garrinm
records.storyText:
The idea comes from Chrome Music Lab, which was addictive and satisfying. I felt it could be that fun and easy to put down musical ideas and hear them grow into something more substantial. Simple at first, but with progressively more depth if the player wants to go there. That was the seed, and it spiraled from there into Jam.

You start with one instrument, and you write parts on a piano roll. Create your own music or play gigs (levels) to earn coins and buy more gear. Each gig is built around one musical idea, so you pick up some music knowledge as you go. Friends can join your studio with a link and write parts alongside you.

In my other Show HNs I've always come with my own code. In this case I didn't write the code, but I'm still proud of the outcome and I hope some of you will enjoy it too.

The audio code is Rust/WASM running in a worklet. This is the part I had prior experience in, and it's been fun getting that into a browser. The instruments are decent and the signal chains hold their own. The front end is the agent's own design in three.js. The optimization work there was interesting because of how busy the UI gets and how many elements come into view. I focused on measuring React renders per interaction, instruction counts for the audio engine, load times and frame times. The result is something that runs decently even on a phone.

The multiplayer side is simple. Each studio is a Cloudflare Durable Object that holds the song. Players connect to it over a WebSocket and send small actions (add a note, turn a knob). The object applies each action, stores the result and sends the updated session to anyone else in the room. This simple setup allows collaborative music making out of the gate, even though it's not the game's main focus (yet).

This is a beta: feedback, comments and criticisms are all welcome. You can get into the game with no signup, and if you want to save your progress you'll be prompted to enter an email address.
